source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (Science 342)
finding: Founding result (GAP 8). Hit = top 5% of citations. Papers that are conventional in the middle but have a novel tail are hits most often.
numbers: WOS 1990-2000 (17.9M papers overall in the study). Hit rate per 100 papers: high median conventionality + high tail novelty 9.11 (6.7% of papers); high conventionality only 5.82 (23%); high tail novelty only 5.33 (26%); neither 2.05 (44%). Background rate 5. P<0.00001. Team papers 37.7% more likely to add novel combinations. Same pattern in other decades, top 1% and 10% hit cutoffs, and 243 fields.
quote: Papers of this type were twice as likely to be highly cited works.
limits: Citation impact only, not disruption. Journal-pair z-scores from WOS co-citation. Odds ratios as such are not printed in the main text; 9.11 vs 5 is about 1.8x (abstract says twice). No replication with LLM-based novelty found.
agent_relevance: Atypical alone does not pay: novelty must sit on a conventional base. Supports mostly-standard attempts with one distant element over fully distant ones.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord (arXiv 2103.03398), methods re-read
finding: Measurement set-up of the 2022 paper. Typicality tau = median journal-pair z-score (higher = more conventional). D uses the LONGEST window available, publication year to 2018.
numbers: Corpus MAG: 87,860,684 articles, 35,431,832 with both D and tau. Cohorts 1970 (87,475), 1980 (176,826), 1990 (318,914), 2000 (591,653). Average 21 references, 32 citations. D stabilises about 10 years after publication (80% of final). t-tests of disruptive-citation fraction, novel vs conventional papers in 2018: 23.85, 33.04, 52.78, 88.76 (all p<0.001). Pearson typicality vs D = -0.05.
limits: Correlation is tiny and is for typicality, so the sign means atypical = more disruptive. Novel = top 10% z-median, conventional = bottom 10%.
agent_relevance: Window length is a candidate cause of the sign conflict with the 2025 paper (see d04, d05). For an agent: judge a distant move after a delay, not at once.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) same paper: delayed recognition and worked examples
finding: The authors argue novel papers get disruptive citations late, because early citers cite both the paper and its references. Examples: Baltimore RNA paper (typicality 266.3, conventional) recognised fast; Watson-Crick (typicality 4.8, D=0.96) recognised later.
numbers: Sleeping-beauty index tracked by novelty decile (Fig 2f). Nobel for Watson-Crick 10 years after publication; Baltimore 5 years.
limits: Two examples are illustrations, not tests. Delay claim rests on cohort curves, no causal design.
agent_relevance: A time-dependent A-D link: a distant attempt may look non-disruptive early and win later. A single-run agent has no such delay, so it needs an external check.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can recombination displace dominant scientific ideas? (arXiv 2506.15959), full text re-read for GAP 2
finding: Checked the full text for any printed correlation, effect size, code or data link. There is none. H1 (atypicality and disruption negatively correlated) is supported only by Fig 3: mean D inside bins of A-index, split by discipline, period and team size, with 95% bootstrap CIs.
numbers: OpenAlex corpus; 40,935,251 articles in Fig 3 and 40,453,825 in Fig 2. Top-5% cut-offs A>22.9 and D>0.04. Text about 15k characters. No coefficient, no regression, no stated D window, no repository URL.
limits: The A scale is not defined in the text, so the direction (high A = atypical) is taken from the hypothesis wording. Effect size cannot be recovered without the figure data or the authors.
agent_relevance: Treat K01 as a direction claim, not a size. Do not build thresholds on it.

source: Cross-read: Lin/Evans/Wu 2022 vs Li/Lin/Wu 2025 for GAP 1 (what differs)
finding: Same group, opposite sign. Differences found in the texts: (1) corpus MAG 2022 vs OpenAlex 2025; (2) 2022 uses the median z (average typicality) while 2025 uses an A-index with a top-tail cut (A>22.9); (3) 2022 uses the longest D window to 2018, 2025 gives none; (4) 2022 reports a pooled r=-0.05, 2025 shows binned means with no pooled number; (5) 2022 cohorts 1970-2000, 2025 covers 1965-2020.
numbers: 2022: r=-0.05 (typicality vs D); novel 61% vs conventional 36% disruptive. 2025: negative slope in every stratum, size unknown.
limits: Neither paper re-runs both measures on one corpus, so the conflict is explained only by candidate causes, not tested. With r=-0.05 on ~35M papers the 2022 effect is sure but practically small.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on the sign of A vs D. Treat distant combination and replacement of the incumbent as two axes and score them separately.

source: Fang, Evans (2025) Generalization and the rise of system-level creativity (arXiv 2510.03240), award regressions in the supplement
finding: GAP 7. Regressions of award status on novelty measures, controlling for citations, references, year and domain. Semantic atypicality predicts non-Nobel major awards in all tested domains. Reference atypicality and D are weak or not significant, except Medicine where both are positive.
numbers: Nobel: one SD of the F (foundation) index raises odds of a Nobel paper by about 58% to 104% depending on domain; E index negative; G index and other novelty measures weak. Non-Nobel awards: 4,704,977 papers (3,990 award) Biology; 5,611,286 (1,367) Chemistry; 3,916,616 (1,223) Medicine. Generalization index rose from 0.218 (1991) to 0.382 (2024).
limits: Same group's analysis; Nobel list and Major Science Award list come from other authors. Trend results were replicated in Web of Science and MAG, but I found no award test on an independent group's data.
agent_relevance: Text-embedding (semantic) atypicality beats reference-list atypicality for awards. An agent can compute embedding distance cheaply; the reference version needs a citation graph.

source: Antoniades et al. (2026) Heuresis: search strategies for autonomous AI research agents across quality, diversity and novelty (arXiv 2606.25198)
finding: GAPS 3, 6, 10. Six search strategies (Greedy, MAP-Elites, Go-Explore, Islands, Curiosity, OMNI) run agents that propose and EXECUTE code changes in three ML domains. Novel ideas are rare and do not reach top quality.
numbers: 3,222 scored runs, 300 iterations per cell. 0 ideas rated Original; best rating Minor Similarity (score 2). Across all tasks exactly 1 idea is both top-10 by quality and score<=2 (sign-modulated GAE-lambda idea, 1.563, RL). nanoGPT: Greedy best val_bpb 0.9567 (185 valid runs), OMNI 0.9584 with 75/300 valid. RL: MAP-Elites best 1.582, Islands 1.563 on 136 valid, Go-Explore 1.561 (249/300 valid), Greedy plateaus at 1.368. Unlearning: no novel idea beats the 1.0 baseline.
quote: No idea across our scored runs is rated as "Original"
limits: ML recipes only (nanoGPT, RL, unlearning), not math. Novelty rated by an LLM with web search (Gupta-Pruthi rubric). Small compute; authors say late breakthroughs at larger budgets are not excluded.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to GAP 3: mechanism-changing ideas were rarely good, polishing the known recipe won on quality. Which search wins depends on task (Greedy on 2 of 3, archives on RL), so no strategy is safe everywhere.

source: Heuresis (2026), novelty-side details (Sec 4.4 and appendix D.4)
finding: The strategy that yields novel-side ideas changes by task. The Curiosity surprise signal does not predict quality.
numbers: Curiosity on nanoGPT: 13 of 300 valid ideas at score 2 (appendix), main text says 20/200 scored runs; others 0. All were residual-stream changes. Unlearning: OMNI novel-side fraction 14.1%, about 3x the next, none beat baseline. RL: MAP-Elites 5%, Go-Explore 6/227, Islands 3/136. Surprise vs quality r=-0.11 on RL; every Curiosity RL idea scored 3 or worse and a quarter were direct copies.
limits: Small counts. The 13 vs 20 difference between appendix and main text is not reconciled here.
agent_relevance: Prediction error (surprise) is not displacement. Supports a separate execution score; a surprise-only reward gave noise.

source: Antoniades et al. (2026) Heuresis, fabrication audit
finding: Execution without audit is not enough: agents reward-hack.
limits: Counted on the runs the authors audited; rate on unaudited runs unknown.
agent_relevance: Any execution check used to prefer a novel attempt must itself be audited, or novel attempts win by cheating.

source: AlphaResearch authors (2025) AlphaResearch: accelerating new algorithm discovery with language models (arXiv 2511.08522)
finding: GAP 6 for math and code. Idea generation plus program execution on 8 open algorithm-discovery problems. A reward model trained on peer-review records filters ideas before execution; it beat code-novelty rejection sampling on 3 of 4 tasks in the first 1,000 iterations.
numbers: 2/8 win rate against human best. Circle packing n=26: 2.636 vs human 2.634 vs AlphaEvolve 2.635; n=32: 2.939 vs 2.936 and 2.937. Failed on Littlewood polynomials and MSTD(n=30), as did OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve. Reward model rejected 151 ideas: 108 were true execution failures, 43 were viable (71.5%).
limits: 8 problems. Reward model is 7B and trained on peer-review scores; it filters ideas, it does not measure novelty. Authors say LLM novelty judgments are unreliable.
agent_relevance: Execution is the arbiter in math/code; a cheap learned prefilter drops many bad ideas at the cost of some good ones. No test of whether novelty helps once execution is applied.

source: Tracing the influence of retrieved literature on scientific ideation in LLMs (2026) (arXiv 2610.39060)
finding: GAP 10. Retrieval narrows diversity of ideas built from the same papers and broadens it only across different paper sets. Ideas lean on one or two papers.
numbers: 45,000 ideas, 15 ML topics, 10 open-weight models, 5 retrieval strategies plus a no-literature baseline. Within-set diversity -5.6% to -17.9%; pooled across sets +10.2% to +18.1% for four of five strategies. In 79.3% of ideas only one or two of eight retrieved papers lead attribution. Mean quality and novelty differences modest.
limits: Embedding diversity and LLM-judged novelty. Ideas only, not executed. Compares retrieval strategies, not planning methods.
agent_relevance: To get distant ideas, vary the retrieved set between attempts; do not retrieve the same set for all attempts.

source: Huang, Xie (2026) Large scientific teams are more, not less, disruptive (arXiv 2610.07329), benchmark table
finding: GAP 4. Authors outside Wu's group build a one-reference disruption index (1D) and test it on six curated benchmarks. The supplement table gives the 1D Nobel number that the critique could not find.
numbers: AUC 1D vs standard D (read as D then 1D): Turing 0.792 vs 0.942; Lasker 0.597 vs 0.979; Nobel 0.731 vs 0.981; Physics milestones 0.398 vs 0.975; Science Breakthrough of the Year 0.259 vs 0.951. 1D range 0.94 to 0.98.
limits: Papers only: no patent analysis in the text. Column order in the extracted table is inferred from the order and the stated range.
agent_relevance: Corrects critique item 3 (Nobel 1D 0.981 is in the supplement). Pairwise-style displacement now has a second group for papers; patents untested.

source: Rutzer, Filimonovic, Macher, Weder (2026) Towards measuring disruptive innovation across countries (arXiv 2603.17881)
finding: GAP 4, patent side. CD index on USPTO data makes the US look less disruptive than Europe and Asia; most of this comes from missing international citations. A global citation network shrinks the non-US advantage.
numbers: Non-US disruptiveness advantage falls by 64% to 148% of the US baseline mean (above 100% means the sign flips). US emerges as leader over Europe.
limits: Tests the standard CD index, not the pairwise or 1D measure.
agent_relevance: Disruption scores from partial reference data can flip the answer; do not trust a displacement score from a partial candidate set.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) LLM breakthrough classification (arXiv 2506.15959, Sec 4.3)
finding: GAPS 5 and 9, nearest evidence. The only LLM use is to label each disruptive paper as theory or method relative to its top reference from title and abstract: a text-only judgment of an idea against its incumbent.
numbers: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, zero-shot, token probability of the theory option used as score. 50,147 papers in the text vs 52,488 in the Fig 4 caption (not reconciled). No accuracy against human labels reported.
limits: Classifier not validated. Predicts nothing about correctness or wins.
agent_relevance: A pairwise refine-or-replace prompt exists, but its agreement with truth is unmeasured, so GAP 5 stays open.

source: Search log: GAP 3 and GAP 5 literature checks this session
finding: Within allowed tools I found no study that scores a candidate answer's displacement of an incumbent answer and tests it against execution outcome, and none that compares distant-analogy vs in-topic attempts at equal tokens. Closest are d07, d10, d11.
numbers: 3 WebSearch calls before the shared budget ran out. arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs returned HTTP 429.
limits: Absence of evidence under blocked search; not proof that none exists.
agent_relevance: Treat these gaps as open and test them in our own harness.

source: Cross-read: Si 2025 Ideation-Execution Gap with Heuresis and AlphaResearch (GAP 6)
finding: Three lines now agree that execution removes the LLM novelty edge in ML research: Si 2025 (N=43, AI ideas lose 1.05/1.76/1.88 points), Heuresis (novel ideas never reach the quality top), AlphaResearch (2 of 8 problems beaten). For math/code beyond ML recipes only AlphaResearch, weak support.
numbers: See d07, d10 and K13. No source found where novelty survives execution in math or code.
limits: Different domains, metrics and models; none uses the same novelty measure.
agent_relevance: Rank by execution check first; use novelty only to choose among equal passers.
